sections.markdown:
## C — Signs and signals part two: red, yellow and green lights and arrows, turns on red, pedestrian signals, lane use control signals and ramp meters, white and yellow pavement lines, turn, center, reversible and carpool lanes, and traffic officer signals
Knowledge domain: what each color and pattern of traffic light, arrow and lane signal tells a Minnesota driver to do, what white and yellow pavement lines allow, how turn, center, reversible and carpool lanes work, and how to follow an officer directing traffic. The manual pairs these with pictures; only the printed text is used here.

FACT_ID: sec10-F01 | anchor: A01
A steady red light means stop: halt at the stop line, before the crosswalk or before entering the intersection, and wait for the light to change. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F02 | anchor: A01
After stopping for a red light you may turn right once the intersection is clear and traffic is allowed in that direction, unless a No Turn on Red sign tells you to wait for green. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F03 | anchor: A01
On red you may turn left from a one-way road onto a one-way cross street only after a full stop, once the intersection is clear, after yielding to pedestrians and vehicles, and only if traffic on the new street moves solely in the direction you are turning. [A01]
Why it matters: the one-way to one-way condition is the key test detail.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F04 | anchor: A01
A red arrow means stop at the stop line, before the crosswalk or before the intersection, and you may go in the arrow's direction only when it turns green. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F05 | anchor: A01
At a flashing red light, stop completely, yield to vehicles and pedestrians who got to the intersection before you, and continue when it is clear. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F06 | anchor: A01
A steady yellow light or arrow means the signal is about to turn red, so do not enter the intersection if you can stop safely, and otherwise go through with caution. [A01]
Why it matters: steady yellow does not mean speed up.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F07 | anchor: A01
If you are waiting in the intersection to turn when the light goes from yellow to red, finish the turn as soon as it is safe, and do not back up. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0069]

FACT_ID: sec10-F08 | anchor: A02
A flashing yellow light or arrow means go through with caution and yield to vehicles and pedestrians already in the intersection. [A02]
Why it matters: flashing yellow left turns are a frequent test item.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-F09 | anchor: A02
On a flashing yellow, a driver turning left or making a U-turn must yield to oncoming vehicles near enough to be an immediate hazard. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-F10 | anchor: A02
On a green light you may cross once the intersection is clear, but you still yield to vehicles or pedestrians in it, to oncoming traffic when turning left, and to pedestrians crossing in front of you when turning either way. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-F11 | anchor: A02
A green arrow means you may turn in its direction, and the turn should be protected from oncoming or crossing traffic. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-F12 | anchor: A02
Pedestrians must obey pedestrian signals, and when the Walk signal shows they should still check that crossing is safe, then may finish crossing once they have started. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-F13 | anchor: A02
When the raised hand or Don't Walk signal flashes, pedestrians should not start crossing, but anyone already in the intersection may finish at a normal pace. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-F14 | anchor: A02
When the raised hand or Don't Walk signal is steady, pedestrians should not try to cross, and anyone already crossing should get to the nearest safe spot as quickly and safely as they can. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0070]

FACT_ID: sec10-F15 | anchor: A03
Lane use control signals let the same lane carry traffic from different directions at different times, and you must still follow every other sign and signal that applies. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F16 | anchor: A03
A steady downward green arrow over a lane means you may drive in that lane. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F17 | anchor: A03
A steady yellow X over a lane means a lane-control change is under way, so prepare to move safely into another lane before a steady red X appears. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F18 | anchor: A03
A flashing yellow X over a lane means you may use it to turn left, with caution, because drivers from the other direction may be turning left in the same lane. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F19 | anchor: A03
A steady downward yellow arrow over a freeway lane means that lane will close, so prepare to move safely into another lane. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F20 | anchor: A03
A flashing downward yellow arrow over a freeway lane means you may use the lane, but with caution. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F21 | anchor: A03
A steady red X over a lane means you may not drive in that lane. [A03]
Why it matters: red X is the only lane signal that bans the lane outright.
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F22 | anchor: A03
At a metered freeway ramp only one car may go on each green light, so drivers take turns entering the highway. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0071]

FACT_ID: sec10-F23 | anchor: A04
White lines separate lanes of traffic moving in the same direction. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F24 | anchor: A04
White dashed lines mean you may change lanes, while shorter, thicker white dashes mean the lane is ending. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F25 | anchor: A04
A solid white line means you should not change lanes, and solid white lines also mark crosswalks, stop lines, parking stalls and the edges of the road. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F26 | anchor: A04
Double solid white lines mean you must not change lanes. [A04]
Why it matters: solid versus double white is a common marking item.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F27 | anchor: A04
A solid white line with a bicycle symbol marks space only for bicycles and electric-assist bicycles, and riders there must travel the same direction as the traffic beside them. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F28 | anchor: A04
Yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F29 | anchor: A04
A solid yellow line means you must not pass, while yellow dashes mean you may pass. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F30 | anchor: A04
Where a solid yellow line runs on one side and dashes on the other, follow the marking on your own lane's side. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F31 | anchor: A04
Double solid yellow lines forbid passing no matter which side of them you are driving on. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0072]

FACT_ID: sec10-F32 | anchor: A05
On a road with two lanes each way separated by two solid yellow lines, do not cross those lines to pass. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0073]

FACT_ID: sec10-F33 | anchor: A06
White turn arrows near intersections, sometimes with the word only, mean a vehicle in that lane must turn, though some lanes show several arrows that allow turning or going straight. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec10-F34 | anchor: A06
Solid white lines separate turn lanes from through lanes to discourage lane changes close to the intersection. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec10-F35 | anchor: A06
A center left-turn-only lane between opposing traffic is marked by parallel solid and dashed yellow lines, sometimes with white arrows, and drivers from either direction may use it to turn left onto a road or driveway. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec10-F36 | anchor: A06
Reversible lanes, used to keep rush-hour traffic moving, are bounded by dashed double yellow lines that you may cross only when the overhead signal for the lane shows a green arrow or a sign allows it. [A06]
Why it matters: reversible versus center turn lane markings are easy to swap.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec10-F37 | anchor: A06
Carpool lanes are only for vehicles with two or more occupants, are marked with a diamond or Carpool Only signs, and usually sit on the far left of a freeway. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec10-F38 | anchor: A06
When an officer is directing traffic, obey the officer's hand signals instead of the traffic signals, signs or pavement markings. [A06]
Why it matters: officer over signal is a classic priority item.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec10-F39 | anchor: A06
Most traffic officers signal stop by raising one hand with the palm toward the vehicle and giving one long whistle blast. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

FACT_ID: sec10-F40 | anchor: A06
Officers signal you to start or keep moving with a hand motion and a series of short whistle blasts, and may use a flashlight when light is low. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0074]

Misconceptions: a steady yellow light is a warning to stop if you safely can, not a signal to hurry through; a green light does not remove the duty to yield to pedestrians and oncoming traffic; a flashing yellow arrow is not a protected turn; an officer's hand signal overrides a green light.
Mnemonics: green arrow guarded, flashing yellow yield; steady yellow X get out, flashing yellow X turn left, red X keep out; one long whistle stop, short whistles go; dashes allow, solids forbid, doubles forbid for everyone.
Glossary: lane use control signal means an overhead light above a lane that shows whether the lane may be used; ramp meter means a signal on a freeway entrance ramp that releases one car per green; reversible lane means a lane whose direction changes, often for rush hour; protected turn means a turn made on a green arrow that should be shielded from oncoming or crossing traffic; carpool lane means a lane limited to vehicles with at least two people.

corpus_stability.reason: The Minnesota Driver’s Manual prints a single edition line (June 2026) on its front cover and opens with a New laws and information chapter that collects recent changes in one place, with no sign of more than one rewrite per year in the selected pages.
